prompt: Where are you in your working life right now?
help: There is no wrong answer. This only changes how we talk about next steps.

prompt: In a sentence or two, what would a good next chapter look like?
help: Income, meaning, a change of pace, a first job — say it in your own words.

prompt: I get genuinely curious when I run into an idea I have not met before.
I would rather stick with a familiar routine than experiment with a new way of doing things.
I finish what I start, even when the last stretch is tedious.
My plans often drift, and unfinished work piles up more than I like.
Being around people for a stretch of time leaves me more energized than drained.
I recover best with quiet, and large groups cost me more than they give.
I instinctively look for the other person's point of view, even in a disagreement.
I tend to put my own needs first and let other people look after theirs.
I stay relatively steady when plans change or pressure rises.
I replay worries more than most people I know, even after the moment has passed.
I enjoy work that involves tools, materials, machines, or the physical world.
I like solving practical problems I can see and touch — a broken thing, a space, a process.
Outdoor, hands-on, or technical work sounds more alive to me than a day of meetings.
I like digging into a question until I understand how it actually works.
Analyzing information, running experiments, or building models sounds like a good day.
I would rather research a hard problem than sell, host, or perform.
I want work that lets me make something original — words, images, spaces, or experiences.
I care about craft, taste, and how something feels, not only whether it functions.
A role with room to invent, write, design, or compose appeals more than a fixed script.
I am drawn to work that helps people learn, heal, or feel less alone.
Listening well and supporting someone through a change is work I respect — and want.
Teaching, counseling, coaching, or community work sounds like a natural fit.
I like taking the lead, pitching an idea, and getting other people moving.
Starting a project, a venture, or a campaign energizes me more than refining a system.
Persuading, negotiating, and owning outcomes sounds like real work to me.
I like bringing order to information — records, schedules, processes, details.
Clear procedures and well-kept systems make me feel competent, not boxed in.
I would rather make a process reliable than invent a brand-new one every week.
Writing — reports, stories, emails that actually land.
Speaking — presenting, facilitating, explaining out loud.
Numbers — estimates, models, careful quantitative reasoning.
Programming — code, scripts, computational tools.
Visual design — layout, form, how something looks and feels.
Research — finding sources, weighing evidence, synthesizing.
Teaching and mentoring — helping someone else get better.
Leadership — setting direction and taking responsibility for a group.
Project management — planning, sequencing, and shipping.
Listening and empathy — hearing what people need, including the unsaid.
Persuasion — selling an idea, a product, or a change.
Hands-on / technical work — tools, materials, bodies, machines, spaces.
Data literacy — reading charts, cleaning data, spotting patterns.
Creative problem-solving — inventing options that were not on the list.
Systems thinking — seeing how parts connect and where the leverage is.
Languages and cross-cultural work.
How much do you need autonomy — choosing how the work gets done?
How much do you need to see the impact of your work on people or a cause?
How much do you need stability — durable demand, predictable structure?
How important is income potential over the next decade?
How much do you need creative expression in the work itself?
How much do you want to work closely with other people, not mostly alone?
How much do you need a field that keeps stretching what you know?
How important is a life with real room outside the job?
